key_terms.meaning: A flaw in code, design or a document that may lead to a failure.
A set of inputs, preconditions and expected results that checks one behaviour.
A source that gives the expected result of a test, such as a specification or a trusted older version.
Checks that a work product matches its specification: 'Are we building the product right?'
Checks that the product meets the user's real need: 'Are we building the right product?'
A white-box method that selects a small set of independent control-flow paths to exercise.
V(G) = E − N + 2, where E is edges and N is nodes of a connected control-flow graph; it gives the number of independent paths.
Divides inputs into classes that should behave alike, so one test per class is enough.
Tests values at and just outside the edges of input classes, where defects cluster.
Tests one module in isolation, usually with a driver and stubs.
Tests whether modules work together through their interfaces in a chosen order.
Tests the complete integrated product against requirements in a production-like environment.
Tests whether the customer will accept the product for use, often against business scenarios.
Reruns selected existing tests after a change to show that unchanged behaviour still works.
Finds the parts of the system a change can affect, so regression tests can be chosen.
Measures response time and throughput under a defined workload.
Pushes the system beyond its capacity to see how it fails and recovers.
Designs tests from classes, inheritance and object state rather than only from functions.
Tests the sequence of requests and server-side state that a web user carries across pages.
Tests an app on devices, networks and interruptions such as calls and low battery.

takeaways: Testing compares expected and actual behaviour; passing tests never proves that defects are absent.
Verification checks the specification, validation checks the user need; QA works on the process, QC on the product.
White-box testing uses control flow; basis path testing gives a small set of independent paths to cover.
Black-box testing uses the specification; equivalence partitioning and boundary values choose efficient inputs.
Unit testing needs drivers and stubs; integration testing needs an order and interface checks.
System testing checks the whole product; acceptance testing checks whether the customer will use it.
Debugging finds and repairs the cause after a failure; it is not the same as testing.
Regression testing after every change protects unchanged behaviour.
Non-functional tests measure speed, capacity, configuration fit and ease of use.
OO, web and mobile systems need tests for state, sessions, devices and networks.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask for definitions with a diagram, a worked control-flow or boundary-value example, and a comparison of testing levels or strategies.

bank.q: Define error, fault, defect and failure. Explain why testing can reveal defects but cannot prove their absence.
outline: Chain from human error to fault to defect to failure
Test oracle and expected versus actual behaviour
Passing tests show only tested behaviour
Defect clustering and limits of sampling

bank.q: Distinguish verification from validation and quality assurance from quality control. Give one example of each.
outline: Static review example and dynamic test example
V-model link between the two pairs

bank.q: Explain basis path testing. Define cyclomatic complexity and show how independent paths are listed from a control-flow graph.
outline: Design one test case per path
Use of a worked small graph

bank.q: Explain equivalence partitioning and boundary value analysis with one input example. Why are boundaries more defect-prone?
outline: Boundaries at min−1, min, min+1, max−1, max, max+1
Example table of inputs and expected results
Reasons boundaries fail: off-by-one, limits, loops

bank.q: A module reads three integers and returns their maximum. Draw a control-flow graph, compute cyclomatic complexity, list independent paths and design test cases.
An online form accepts an age from 18 to 60. Using equivalence partitioning and boundary value analysis, list test inputs and expected results.
outline: Test table with expected accept or reject

bank.q: Explain unit testing with a driver and a stub. Design a unit test plan for a module that calculates a railway fare.
outline: Driver calls the module under test
Test cases for normal, boundary and invalid inputs

bank.q: Compare top-down, bottom-up, sandwich and big-bang integration. Choose an order for a system with a user interface, business logic and database layer.
After a change in a tax calculation module, explain impact analysis and compare retest-all, random selection and safe selection for regression testing.
outline: Random selection is cheap but risky
Safe selection follows data and control dependencies

bank.q: Describe performance, load, stress and soak testing for an online ticket-booking site. Define response time and throughput.
outline: Response time from request to reply

bank.q: Evaluate a test strategy for a mobile banking app. Cover unit, integration, system, acceptance, regression, usability, accessibility and device testing.
outline: Unit and integration for transfer logic
System and acceptance for business scenarios
Usability and accessibility for real users

bank.q: Analyse why defects escape to production even when unit and integration tests pass. Discuss test oracle limits, coverage, regression selection and non-functional gaps.
outline: Oracle may be wrong or incomplete
Coverage may miss paths and data
Non-functional gaps such as load and configuration
Preventive reviews and better test design

bank.q: Compare white-box and black-box testing. Explain when each is effective and how basis path testing and equivalence partitioning complement each other.
outline: Combining basis paths with boundary inputs

bank.q: Evaluate the testing challenges of object-oriented, web and mobile applications. Propose a test approach for each challenge.
outline: Web sessions, cookies and server state

glossary.def: Testing without a planned design, often to explore a suspicion.
A focused team session that hunts defects in one build or feature.
A record of a defect with steps to reproduce, expected and actual results, and status.
A human mistake that puts a fault into a work product.
A flaw in code or design that can cause a failure.
The observed departure of system behaviour from expected behaviour.
A collection of test cases run together.
Software and data that run unit tests and report results.
A simple replacement for a called module that returns fixed data.
A test program that calls the module under test and passes inputs.
The process of finding and repairing the cause of a failure.
An author reads code or design line by line with a colleague.
An author leads a team through a work product to find problems.
A formal review with defined roles, a checklist and recorded defects.
A review of source code for defects and standards.
Testing that examines work products without running code.
Testing that runs code and observes behaviour.
Any document, model, code or test artefact produced in development.
Running every existing test after a change.
Choosing regression tests by tracing data and control dependencies from the change.
The value below which 95 percent of measured responses fall.
The number of transactions a system completes per unit time.
Checks that people with disabilities can use the product.
Checks that the product works with specified browsers, operating systems and hardware.
Observes real users doing tasks to find difficulties.
Runs the system at load for a long time to find leaks and degradation.
